title: Start here: pick skills by task
why: One tiny map keeps every other skill small: the agent reads hundreds of tokens, not thousands.
prompt: Create and install a skill named `code-index` (Start here: pick skills by task). It instructs the agent as follows: Your installed skills each do one job — never read them all. Three skills apply to almost every task, so always read these: code-secure, code-reuse, code-token. Then match the task and read only the matched skills: new screen or page → ui-shell, ui-tokens. New interactive piece (typing, dragging, live numbers) → ui-framework as well. Mobile app build → ui-mobile. New service or script → code-language, code-shape. Organizing a new codebase → code-group. Services in other languages → code-boundaries. Login, accounts, permissions → code-auth. Security deep-dives, read on match: code-crypto, code-injection, code-design, code-misconfig, code-deps, code-integrity, code-logging, code-ssrf. Page behavior and states → ui-behavior. Headers and navigation → ui-nav. These stack picks assume a new codebase: if the project already uses something else — another language, framework, or tokens — follow that instead. The house rule beats the skill. Skip everything else. When building is done → verify-tests, and verify-visual for anything with a screen. Missing a skill? Copy its prompt from the board once, install it, then use it locally. This follows progressive disclosure, the Agent Skills model — map first, details on demand: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/equipping-agents-for-the-real-world-with-agent-skills
checks: whole bank never copied at once

title: Python first, house wins
why: Frameworks make whole mistake classes unwritable, so the agent spends tokens on the task instead of on validation and plumbing.
prompt: Create and install a skill named `code-language` (Python first, house wins). It instructs the agent as follows: Default to Python — agents generate it fastest, with the fewest mistakes. Write services with FastAPI + Pydantic: one model drives routing, validation, and the OpenAPI schema — never hand-write type checks. One SQLModel class serves as both table and validator. CLIs are one Typer-decorated function. Type everything; let the framework and tests catch errors, not code review. If the codebase already uses another language, do not create this skill at all — skip it. Framework first: use the framework's own piece for anything it covers; hand-write only what no framework covers. Between same-language services reuse the same models; when sibling services differ, use gRPC between services and keep the edge framework at the edge. If the project already uses a different stack, overwrite this skill with that stack's equivalent and follow it instead.
checks: tests cover happy path + one edge

title: Mobile: FastAPI + HTMX + Tailwind + Capacitor
why: One language and zero client state means the agent writes every feature once and it ships to both app stores.
prompt: Create and install a skill named `ui-mobile` (Mobile: FastAPI + HTMX + Tailwind + Capacitor). It instructs the agent as follows: Build mobile apps as server-rendered HTML: FastAPI routes return fragments, HTMX attributes (hx-get/hx-target) give SPA behavior with near-zero JavaScript, Tailwind utilities handle responsive layout inline, Capacitor wraps the mobile viewport into iOS/Android shells. No client state, no fetch calls, no Swift/Kotlin.  If the project already uses a different mobile stack, do not create this skill at all — skip it.

title: Token-efficient code
why: Every token spent writing or re-reading code is a token not spent on the task; cheap code compounds across sessions.
prompt: Create and install a skill named `code-token` (Token-efficient code). It instructs the agent as follows: Write code that's cheap to generate and cheap to re-read: type everything, one canonical pattern per job (FastAPI route, Pydantic model, Typer command). Early returns, table-driven branches over nested ifs, JSON-first data. Delete dead code — every dead line taxes every future read. Prefer 20 lines of plain code over 5 lines of clever code.

title: Secure by default
why: Insecure code fails late and expensively; validated boundaries fail fast on the first bad input.
prompt: Create and install a skill named `code-secure` (Secure by default). It instructs the agent as follows: Validate every input at the boundary

title: Login and permissions
why: Authentication is the most-broken OWASP category; one shared login path removes the whole class.
prompt: Create and install a skill named `code-auth` (Login and permissions). It instructs the agent as follows: Logins use signed cookies (built into Starlette — one secret key, no extra package). Sign in with Google uses authlib. Services talking to each other use JWTs via pyjwt. Passwords are checked with bcrypt via passlib — never write your own password check, because a wrong one fails silently and an agent will not notice. For every action, check the permission at the boundary and default to deny: never trust a role or user id sent by the client, always re-check it on the server.
checks: permission checked per action, default deny

title: No homegrown crypto
why: Homegrown crypto fails silently; platform crypto fails loudly and rarely.
prompt: Create and install a skill named `code-crypto` (No homegrown crypto). It instructs the agent as follows: Use vetted crypto only: TLS for data in motion, platform encryption (KMS, age, or libsodium) for data at rest — never a hand-rolled cipher. Secrets live in environment variables, never in code or logs. Passwords are hashed, not encrypted (see code-auth); API tokens are random, scoped, and expire.
checks: no secret in code or logs

title: Input stays data
why: Injection is input treated as instructions; parameters keep input as data.
prompt: Create and install a skill named `code-injection` (Input stays data). It instructs the agent as follows: Never build queries, commands, or markup by gluing strings around user input. Database reads go through the ORM (SQLModel parameterizes everything). Templates auto-escape HTML — never mark user content safe. OS commands, LDAP, and XPath get the same rule: parameters, never concatenation.

title: Abuse story first
why: Missing controls can't be patched in later without redesigning the feature.
prompt: Create and install a skill named `code-design` (Abuse story first). It instructs the agent as follows: For each feature, ask how it is abused before asking how it is used: who pays for heavy use, who is hurt by bad input. Default to deny, grant least privilege, rate-limit costly endpoints, and cap upload and response sizes. A feature without an abuse story is not designed yet.

title: Safe settings shipped
why: Most breaches walk through doors the defaults left open.
prompt: Create and install a skill named `code-misconfig` (Safe settings shipped). It instructs the agent as follows: Ship with the safe settings on: debug and trace off in production, generic error pages that leak nothing, strict transport security and a content security policy, CORS allowlists instead of wildcards, and no default passwords or open admin pages. Review headers and flags on every deploy, not once.

title: Dependencies audited
why: Your code inherits every vulnerability in every library it imports.
prompt: Create and install a skill named `code-deps` (Dependencies audited). It instructs the agent as follows: Pin every dependency (requirements with versions), audit on a schedule (pip audit or equal), and update promptly when a fix lands. Fewer dependencies means fewer advisories: drop what the stack already covers. Never vendor a copy you will forget to patch.

title: Verify before trust
why: A build that can't prove what it contains can't prove what it ships.
prompt: Create and install a skill named `code-integrity` (Verify before trust). It instructs the agent as follows: Trust nothing you didn't verify: lockfiles pin the whole tree, webhook handlers check signatures before acting, CI runs tests before deploys, and installs come from registries — never pipe a URL to a shell. If bytes changed without a commit, stop and ask.

title: Logs that catch break-ins
why: You can't respond to an attack you never recorded or never noticed.
prompt: Create and install a skill named `code-logging` (Logs that catch break-ins). It instructs the agent as follows: Log the events that catch break-ins: failed logins, validation failures, permission denials, and spikes in costly endpoints. Keep logs structured (who, what, when) and secret-free — logs get copied and shared. Watch them with an alert, not just storage: an unread log is decoration.
checks: alerts on spikes, not just storage

title: Server fetches allowlisted
why: A server that fetches arbitrary URLs becomes a proxy into your own network.
prompt: Create and install a skill named `code-ssrf` (Server fetches allowlisted). It instructs the agent as follows: Never fetch a user-supplied URL from the server without an allowlist: block internal addresses and cloud metadata (169.254.169.254), resolve and re-check the host, and cap timeouts and response sizes. Prefer webhooks and signed callbacks over server-side fetching whenever the design allows.

title: Service boundaries
why: The wrong protocol between services costs speed forever; the right one is a one-line decision made once.
prompt: Create and install a skill named `code-boundaries` (Service boundaries). It instructs the agent as follows: Connect services by rule, not habit: same Python system → shared Pydantic models over HTTP; other languages or hot internal paths → protobuf plus gRPC, FastAPI stays at the edge; events and queues → Pydantic-validated messages. Build the whole app in Python by default, but carve out other languages where Python technically fails: single-digit-millisecond budgets use Go or Rust, over 100k live connections use Erlang or Elixir, heavy offline clients and games and widgets go native.
checks: protocol chosen by rule, not default
non-Python parts named with their technical reason
FastAPI at the edge in mixed systems

title: UI shell in 40 lines
why: Humans get the interface they prefer; metadata makes it legible to agents without dumbing it down.
prompt: Create and install a skill named `ui-shell` (UI shell in 40 lines). It instructs the agent as follows: Build mobile-first: design at 360px width, then scale up — full-monitor layouts only when the task genuinely needs a big screen. Semantic HTML shell (<header>/<main>/<footer>), one stylesheet, no UI framework. System font stack, 2 colors + 1 accent, 4px spacing scale. Humans get the UI they prefer — icon-only buttons and custom controls included — but every control must expose machine-readable metadata: a real <button>/<a>/<input>, a visible label or aria-label, and a data-action naming what it does. Pull icons from Lucide: `<i data-lucide='name'>` plus one `lucide.createIcons()` call; never hand-write SVG paths — the agent picks icon names, not pixels. Hand-drawn icons burn tokens and time for a worse result: Lucide is already in the model's training so the agent knows every name, and already familiar to users so people recognize each icon on sight.
checks: every control has a label or aria-label

title: Tokens + Tailwind
why: Fixing palette and spacing to tokens removes an entire category of per-element decisions.
prompt: Create and install a skill named `ui-tokens` (Tokens + Tailwind). It instructs the agent as follows: Style with Tailwind utilities for layout and spacing, on top of three color tokens (--ink, --paper, --accent) and a 4/8/16/32 scale. Keep preflight on as the consistent baseline — describe every margin, bullet, and underline explicitly, never rely on browser defaults. Two neutrals plus one accent, 1px borders, radii 6px/10px. Contrast >= 4.5:1 so the human eyeball verdict works.  If the project already uses a different design system, do not create this skill at all — skip it.

title: Behavior contract
why: Explicit text states make every outcome checkable by agents and humans alike, with no interpretation needed.
prompt: Create and install a skill named `ui-behavior` (Behavior contract). It instructs the agent as follows: Every mutation needs an explicit state: idle → working → done|error. Show text status, never color alone. Respect prefers-reduced-motion. Confirm destructive actions inline. Humans verify by looking; log the state string for agents.
checks: each action exposes a text status

title: Machine-shaped modules
why: Small typed modules fit in a single read, so the agent holds the whole unit in context at once.
prompt: Create and install a skill named `code-shape` (Machine-shaped modules). It instructs the agent as follows: Write small flat Python modules: one file, one job, <150 lines. Typed inputs and outputs (Pydantic in, response_model out), no hidden globals, no clever abstractions. Flat over nested (depth <= 2, early returns). Raise HTTPException at boundaries; never leak tracebacks or raw errors. Name files by what they do: skills.py, validate.py, render.py.

title: Tests are the spec
why: Tests are the only verdict both humans and agents can trust without reading the code.
prompt: Create and install a skill named `verify-tests` (Tests are the spec). It instructs the agent as follows: Humans judge by tests, not by reading code. Ship one runnable check per behavior: one command (`./run.sh test`, `pytest`) must pass. Cover happy path + one edge (empty, oversized, unauthorized). Print PASS/FAIL lines an agent can parse.

title: Visual confirmation
why: A screenshot settles in one glance what no code review can prove about a UI.
prompt: Create and install a skill named `verify-visual` (Visual confirmation). It instructs the agent as follows: Humans judge UI by looking. Every screen needs a settled screenshot state with real data (no lorem, no empty list). List the 3 things to eyeball: layout, labels, error state. Save verification screenshots to the project's shots/ folder (gitignored), named for what they show — never /tmp. Never trust a headless screenshot alone: use it for a quick first look only, and treat a real browser or the user's own screenshot as proof; when they disagree, believe the user's screen. If it cannot be seen, it does not ship.

title: Reuse before you build
why: Every line the agent doesn't write is tokens never spent and bugs never made.
prompt: Create and install a skill named `code-reuse` (Reuse before you build). It instructs the agent as follows: Before writing anything new, look for a piece that already does the job: search the repo first, then the stack's own library — Flowbite components, Lucide icons, Lit or WebAwesome pieces, FastAPI and Pydantic helpers. Use the found piece as-is and adapt only what the task needs. When the same markup or logic appears twice, pull it into one shared helper or component where the next agent will find it — never paste a third copy. Hand-write only what no existing piece covers.
checks: no hand-built copy of a stocked piece
repeated markup lives in one helper
new pieces placed where agents will find them

title: Group by feature, drop the layers
why: One folder holds the whole component, so the agent reads once instead of hunting across layers.
prompt: Create and install a skill named `code-group` (Group by feature, drop the layers). It instructs the agent as follows: Organize new code by feature, not by layer: a component's files sit together — checkout_routes.py, checkout_models.py, checkout_tests.py — named <feature>_<kind> so everything is found in one place. Keep model/view/controller separation inside the folder, not across the codebase. Put truly shared definitions (Pydantic contracts) in one shared module every feature imports. If the codebase already uses a pattern like MVC, follow that pattern instead: restructuring working code costs tokens and every move risks new errors.
checks: shared facts live in one module

title: Islands first, house wins
why: Standard web components with no build step; every new interactive region starts as one.
prompt: Create and install a skill named `ui-framework` (Islands first, house wins). It instructs the agent as follows: Default to Lit islands for interactive regions, loaded from the pinned Lit CDN module — no build step, no framework lock-in. Lit ships no ready-made pieces, so keep Flowbite for those (menu, dialog, dropdown) and never rebuild one just to own it; if an island needs pieces, use WebAwesome over CDN; never React or Angular. Render into the light DOM (never shadow) so utilities and icons keep working; HTMX never targets an island or anything inside one. If the codebase already uses another framework, do not create this skill at all — skip it. If the project already uses a different stack, overwrite this skill with that stack's equivalent and follow it instead.
checks: light DOM so utilities keep working

title: Responsive headers
why: Navigation is the first thing a visitor meets; if it overflows on a phone the whole site looks broken.
prompt: Create and install a skill named `ui-nav` (Responsive headers). It instructs the agent as follows: Show inline links on wide screens; below about 640px collapse them behind a hamburger button that opens a Flowbite dropdown (data-dropdown-toggle) — the library positions it as an overlay, so the open menu never pushes content down. Use a real nav landmark and a real button with an aria-label; Flowbite flips aria-expanded itself. Put the brand on its own centered row; stack the opened links vertically. No hand-written menu code, keyboard reachable.
checks: keyboard can open and walk the menu
